rv.q: Like its subject, this playful, exuberant theatrical happening wins you over with sheer heart and good humour.

The come-one, come-all spirit of the new venue suits the daffy alchemy of an evening which starts like a potentially alienating in-joke and builds, by degrees and via an ingredient-spattering cooking session, to a shared delirium of life-affirming silliness.

Soon he had become a much-loved, permanent fixture and in 2013 was awarded an honorary degree. He worked for years as a circus clown, parlayed his way into a role at Stoke City football club as kit-man and all-round good luck charm (described by manager Lou Macari as “the best signing I ever made”) and runs his own football club.

I’ve rarely been in a theatre where the spectators seemed to breathe so much in time with a show. This is the more striking as the life it lights up is a specifically Potteries story. Baldwin, who was the subject of a 2014 television film starring Toby Jones, is a famous local figure.

Now it is a distinctive debut for a distinctive space. @sohoplace is the first new purpose-built theatre to arrive in the West End in 50 years. I can’t love the @; everything else looks and sounds great.
This show is about joy, as much as difficulty, and it's refreshing to watch something that celebrates difference without falling into pat sentimentality.

More sophisticated shows will follow, but until then Michael Hugo's 'Nello' is perhaps even better than Toby Jones in the film, as he guides the other six actors through his life story, proudly sporting a British Empire Medal on a loose grey suit, blissfully untroubled by reality. Just as good is Suzanne Ahmet as Neil's devoted Mum.

Diagnosed, as a child, with a learning disability – although, as his devoted mum tartly points out here, “they didn’t call it that then” – Neil was expected to live a life of quiet compromise and limited horizons.
'Marvellous' is one of the first times a West End show seemed to authentically present elements of neurodiversity in both casting and script, while never overly laden with sign-posting or preaching.
You really do need a sunny disposition to love, rather than just admire, this show.

cn.t: Critics praise "Marvellous" for its heartfelt emotional appeal and authentic portrayal of neurodiversity, with the show earning recognition for its inclusive casting and sincere storytelling that avoids preachiness.
